population: US outpatients aged 30 or older with acute COVID-19; Omicron period; vaccination allowed
comparison: Fluvoxamine 50 mg twice on day 1, then 100 mg twice daily for 12 days versus matched placebo
endpoint: Time from study-drug receipt to the third of three consecutive symptom-free days
finding: Higher-dose fluvoxamine did not shorten sustained recovery: adjusted hazard ratio 0.99 (95% Bayesian credible interval 0.89–1.09). Median recovery was 10 days in both groups.
limits: The modified intention-to-treat analysis included 1175 of 1208 randomized participants; 33 without timely drug delivery were excluded after randomization. assessment.rationale: The masked randomized comparison directly informs this symptom-recovery endpoint, and the credible interval is close to no effect. Postrandomization drug-delivery exclusions, participant-reported recovery, a skeptical Bayesian prior and the selected Omicron-era population leave uncertainty about smaller effects and applicability; the result is informative without proving equivalence.

population: Nonhospitalized US adults aged 30–85 with overweight or obesity, positive test within 3 days and symptoms for less than 7 days
comparison: Fluvoxamine 50 mg twice daily for 14 days versus concurrently randomized matched control, adjusted for other factorial assignments
endpoint: Composite of home oxygen saturation at or below 93%, emergency department visit, hospitalization, or death
finding: Fluvoxamine did not demonstrate a reduction in the primary composite: adjusted odds ratio 0.94 (95% CI 0.66–1.36). Complete-case primary events were 79/329 versus 80/321; the adjusted model used multiple imputation.

population: Generally healthy adults aged 50–85; selected health-conscious cohort
comparison: Compounded rapamycin 5 mg or 10 mg once weekly versus placebo
finding: PEARL did not demonstrate a difference in its primary visceral-adiposity outcome. Dose-specific odds ratios for improvement were 1.81 (95% CI 0.73–4.50) at 5 mg and 1.68 (0.66–4.32) at 10 mg; both intervals included no difference.
limits: This was a small completer analysis: 125 randomized, 114 completed (40 at 5 mg, 35 at 10 mg, 39 placebo); missing outcome values were removed pairwise. The compounded formulation had lower measured exposure than commercial sirolimus; nominal study doses cannot be assumed interchangeable with commercial tablets. Healthy, health-conscious adults aged 50–85 were selected; lifespan and prevention of age-related diseases were not established. All authors reported employment and/or ownership interests in AgelessRx.

assessment.rationale: The masked randomized design directly addresses visceral adiposity at 48 weeks, but the small completer-only sample, missing DXA observations, broad intervals and reduced bioavailability of the compounded preparation leave substantial uncertainty. No primary VAT benefit was demonstrated; this surrogate finding cannot establish lifespan extension or rule out an adiposity effect.

domains.name: Study methods
domains.text: Pharmacy-managed randomization and matching capsules kept participants and study staff masked. Eleven randomized participants were excluded as noncompleters; endpoint-specific missingness used pairwise removal, and adherence was largely self-reported.

domains.name: Directness
domains.text: Visceral adiposity was the prespecified primary body-composition endpoint in normative aging, not a validated measure of lifespan extension. The compounded product and selected healthy cohort limit wider applicability.

domains.name: Precision
domains.text: The improvement odds-ratio intervals are broad: 0.73–4.50 at 5 mg and 0.66–4.32 at 10 mg. They do not exclude important differences; a nonsignificant test is not evidence of equivalence.

domains.name: Consistency
domains.text: This is one small three-arm trial, with both doses sharing one placebo group. Dose arms and secondary outcomes are not independent replications, and no pooled longevity estimate is justified.

domains.text: The hashed original PDF and its embedded tables and enrollment schematic were inspected locally; companion files were hash-verified. Authors disclosed AgelessRx employment/ownership and company support. This is local editorial inspection, not independent or human approval.

finding: Women in the 10 mg group had a larger percentage change in lean tissue mass than placebo: between-group difference 6.194 percentage points (95% CI 0.8773–11.5105; Bonferroni-adjusted P = 0.018). This small secondary subgroup finding does not demonstrate longer life or better physical function.
limits: The positive finding is a small secondary sex-specific comparison amid many body-composition and survey analyses; replication and clinical importance remain uncertain. This was a small completer analysis: 125 randomized, 114 completed (40 at 5 mg, 35 at 10 mg, 39 placebo); missing outcome values were removed pairwise. The compounded formulation had lower measured exposure than commercial sirolimus; nominal study doses cannot be assumed interchangeable with commercial tablets. Healthy, health-conscious adults aged 50–85 were selected; lifespan and prevention of age-related diseases were not established. All authors reported employment and/or ownership interests in AgelessRx.

assessment.rationale: The reported between-group lean-tissue contrast favors 10 mg compounded rapamycin in women, but few women contributed, endpoint-specific observations were missing, and this was a secondary subgroup among many analyses. Confidence in a general clinical benefit is low despite the positive adjusted comparison; muscle function, sarcopenia treatment and longevity were not demonstrated.

domains.name: Study methods
domains.text: Pharmacy-managed randomization and matching capsules kept participants and study staff masked. Eleven randomized participants were excluded as noncompleters; endpoint-specific missingness used pairwise removal, and adherence was largely self-reported. The reported pairwise contrast used a multiple-comparison correction, but sex-specific secondary analyses still require cautious interpretation.

domains.name: Directness
domains.text: The direct measurement is baseline-normalized lean tissue on DXA in women, not strength, walking performance, diagnosed sarcopenia or survival. It cannot be generalized to all older adults or other formulations.

domains.name: Precision
domains.text: The 48-week contrast is +6.194 percentage points with 95% CI 0.8773–11.5105. The wide range and small subgroup leave the size and practical significance uncertain; subgroup follow-up N is not fully reconciled here.

domains.name: Consistency
domains.text: A 24-week signal in the same participants is not independent replication. No significant male benefit or benefit across all doses is inferred, and the null primary VAT result remains separately visible.

domains.name: Source integrity
domains.text: The hashed original PDF and its embedded tables and enrollment schematic were inspected locally; companion files were hash-verified. Authors disclosed AgelessRx employment/ownership and company support. This is local editorial inspection, not independent or human approval.

population: Female C57BL/6 mice, treatment beginning at about 20 months, in two research colonies
comparison: Encapsulated rapamycin 42 ppm in chow versus matched eudragit vehicle chow
endpoint: Periodontal bone loss measured by cementoenamel-junction to alveolar-bone-crest distance
finding: Rapamycin-treated aged mice had more periodontal bone than vehicle controls; longitudinal scans in one colony also showed bone gain relative to baseline. This is an animal finding and does not establish periodontal benefit in people.
limits: Only female mice were studied, with small colony-specific groups; human dose, durability and clinical benefit were not established. The experiments measured multiple bone and inflammatory outcomes; a numeric pooled estimate and confidence interval were not extracted.

assessment.rationale: Two controlled mouse cohorts and repeated imaging support an experimental bone finding, but small female-only groups, model-specific exposures and incomplete reporting of allocation concealment prevent a confident human clinical inference. The evidence is explicitly preclinical, with no human trial count, treatment effect or benefit letter.

domains.name: Study methods
domains.text: Vehicle controls and two colonies strengthen the experiment; JAX imaging was longitudinal and image landmarking used randomized images and independent observers. Allocation concealment and complete investigator blinding were not established in this appraisal.

domains.name: Directness
domains.text: These are aged female mouse periodontal-bone measurements, not clinical attachment, tooth retention or symptoms in patients. Dietary concentration cannot be translated into a human therapeutic dose.

domains.name: Precision
domains.text: NIA-UW had 10 old mice per treatment and JAX 13 per treatment. Directional findings were reported with tests and plots; a numeric effect and interval were not extracted, so no magnitude is asserted.

domains.name: Consistency
domains.text: Concordant findings at two sites within one report improve experimental coherence but are not independent human replication. Different colonies and imaging designs remain separate.

domains.name: Source integrity
domains.text: The exact hashed full-text XML contains methods, figures/captions and the published peer-review exchange. No retraction flag was seen in these local bytes; no new current integrity search or independent review was performed.

population: Human colorectal cancer cell lines and primary cells; xenografts in female nude mice
comparison: Ivermectin in cyclodextrin versus carrier; TCF-independent and TCFVP16 rescue controls
endpoint: Growth of established colorectal cancer xenografts dependent on WNT-TCF signaling
timepoint: Serial tumor measurements every 2–3 days during treatment
finding: Ivermectin inhibited growth of WNT-TCF-dependent colorectal xenografts; TCF-independent growth was not similarly inhibited, and constitutively active TCF rescued growth. These experiments support a pathway hypothesis rather than clinical colorectal-cancer efficacy.
limits: Preclinical model, nonclinical route and exposure, small experimental groups and incomplete allocation/blinding information prevent a clinical efficacy inference. The exact molecular target remained unresolved; TCF-independent models were not responsive. No clinical survival, response or toxicity benefit was tested.

assessment.rationale: The report links xenograft growth inhibition to TCF dependence using negative and rescue controls, but the findings arise from cell and immunodeficient-mouse models at nonclinical exposures. Small experiments, no human comparator and unresolved translation leave weak support for any clinical colorectal-cancer inference; no A–F clinical benefit grade is assigned.

domains.name: Study methods
domains.text: Carrier controls, TCF-independent models and constitutively active TCF rescue test pathway specificity. The local report did not establish allocation concealment or blinded tumor measurements for this appraisal.

domains.name: Directness
domains.text: Human-derived cells implanted in nude mice remain nonclinical evidence. Daily intraperitoneal exposure is not an oral cancer regimen in patients, and pathway-sensitive lines are a selected subset.

domains.name: Precision
domains.text: Tumor growth was assessed serially with small experiment-level groups. A common numeric effect and confidence interval were not extracted, and no patient denominator or clinical magnitude is available.

domains.name: Consistency
domains.text: TCF-dependent inhibition and rescue are internally coherent, while TCF-independent growth is a material negative result. Multiple assays within one report do not establish replicated clinical benefit.

domains.name: Source integrity
domains.text: The existing full-text XML hash matched its local acquisition manifest and contained experimental methods and figure captions. Supplements/raw experimental datasets were not independently reanalyzed; no fresh integrity search or human approval is claimed.
